title: Is the share of every child the same in these three roti groups?
description: One roti among two children, two rotis among four children and three rotis among six children are compared by cutting every roti into halves. Each child gets one half every time, while Keeko doubts it by looking only at the number of rotis.
teaching_notes: One idea: when the rotis and the children grow together, each share stays the same. Watch for students who compare only the number of rotis and ignore the number of children.

source: Find the share of each child: (a) 1 roti divided equally bet
video_script.why: The child finds the share of one child in three sharing groups and sees that every child gets the same amount of roti.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own rotis shared among 2, 4 and 6 children
video_script.anchor: three mats: one roti with two children, two rotis with four children, three rotis with six children
video_script.wrong_answer: the children with three rotis get the most
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the children with three rotis get the most, because three rotis is the most. That mat also has the most children, six of them sharing, so the rotis must be cut and one child's share looked at.
video_script.payoff_line: Every child gets half a roti, so the shares are the same

final_answer.value: a. 1/2; b. 2/4; c. 3/6. Yes, each child gets half a roti, so 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6.
final_answer.spoken: one half, two fourths and three sixths, and yes, each child gets half a roti

video_script.fraction_reading: one half, two fourths, three sixths
maths_rules: (a) 1 roti among 2 children, (b) 2 rotis among 4 children, (c) 3 rotis among 6 children
(a) 2 halves for 2 children, (b) 4 halves for 4 children, (c) 6 halves for 6 children
each child gets 1 half every time
slip: Keeko thinks the mat with 3 rotis gives the most, but it also has the most children
video_script.design: One idea: cut every roti into halves and look at one child's share. The three mats stay side by side.
